entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Boris Davidovich Berman, a high-ranking officer in the Soviet Union's notorious NKVD (People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs) from the mid-1930s until his own arrest in 1938, was a central figure in the brutal apparatus of state terror that defined the Great Purge. Born in 1900, Berman's career epitomized the rapid rise and precipitous fall characteristic of Stalin's inner circle during this period. As a key administrator and enforcer, he played a direct role in the systematic repression, arrests, and executions that decimated the Soviet military, party leadership, and intelligentsia, thereby profoundly shaping the political landscape of the USSR on the eve of World War II.

Berman's ascent within the NKVD saw him serve in critical roles, including Head of the Fourth Department (Secret Political Department) of the NKVD Main Directorate of State Security (GUGB) from May 1937 to June 1938. In this capacity, he was instrumental in orchestrating the purges of the Red Army, famously overseeing the arrest of Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and other high-ranking military commanders in the so-called 'Case of the Anti-Soviet Trotskyist Military Organization.' His department was responsible for uncovering and suppressing alleged counter-revolutionary plots within the party, government, and armed forces, leading to countless show trials and summary executions. Berman’s direct supervision extended to the widespread arrests of former oppositionists and 'enemies of the people' across various Soviet republics.
